title: King Charles: Pace of AI is ‘deeply concerning’
content:
AYRSHIRE, Scotland — King Charles will say the pace of AI development is “deeply concerning” and tell industry leaders they must provide the public with “reassurance” as he hosts an exclusive gathering on Thursday about the future of the technology.

The event at Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland, first reported by POLITICO, takes place amid heightened global concern over rapid advances in AI.

“The development of AI — its substance and its pace — are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure,” Charles is expected to tell attendees in opening remarks.

He will say that “those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny.”

And he will warn that the “decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations,” calling on attendees “not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”

title: What AI urgency? Industry and leaders split on how to handle advanced tech’s threats
content:
The seeming unanimity among artificial intelligence industry powerhouses about addressing AI’s potential threats to humanity is already splintering.

Four days after OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk locked arms behind a call to slow AI’s advances, a phalanx of industry leaders and lawmakers speaking Wednesday at POLITICO’s Decoded Summit came to no consensus on how to regulate the technology — despite mostly agreeing that it’s a task someone should lead.

Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck declined to endorse the same proposal for congressionally mandated independent AI monitoring that OpenAI had backed the day before. Progressive Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) advocated mandatory limits on the technology and the creation of a federal agency to regulate it, while House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) said speed is less important than getting the policy right — and the two clashed on whether Americans should care about beating China.
snippet: The seeming unanimity among artificial intelligence industry powerhouses about addressing AI’s potential threats to humanity is already splintering.
creator: Katherine Long, Gabby Miller, Owen Dahlkamp

title: ‘The US can’t lose’: Pentagon plows ahead on AI despite warnings
content:
Pentagon leaders are racing to insert artificial intelligence into nearly every corner of the military, even as lawmakers scramble to figure out guardrails.

Defense Department officials insist any slowdown in AI development could cede control to adversaries, dismissing calls from industry leaders and members of Congress to pause and better understand the long-term ramifications of the computer systems.

That tension is playing out in real time as the Pentagon faces increasingly bold threats from China and Russia. But the military’s rush to stay ahead brings separate risks if it fails to safeguard hastily implemented AI tech.

“Winning and staying ahead in the AI race is probably one of the most important things for the United States to do, both from a military and economic security perspective,” Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said. “That is a race that the U.S. can’t lose.”

But critics warn the rush to use advanced AI in national security operations could also open sensitive military systems to new threats, especially if leaders aren’t deliberate about installing defenses during upgrades.
snippet: Pentagon leaders are racing to insert artificial intelligence into nearly every corner of the military, even as lawmakers scramble to figure out guardrails.
creator: Leo Shane III

title: Hugging Face CEO: Advanced AI models require new transparency mandates
content:
victim to history’s first known autonomous artificial intelligence cyberattack said the government should do more to require transparency by advanced AI models — and ensure that their developers are held liable for harms their products cause.

That doesn’t mean Congress needs to create a raft of new regulations prohibiting malicious cyberattacks, Hugging Face CEO and co-founder Clem Delangue said Wednesday during the POLITICO Decoded Summit in D.C. But he said companies whose products inflict damage should not be able to dodge responsibility.

“I think it’s too easy to say: ‘OK, it was an agent. That did the bad thing and so no one is responsible,’” Delangue said. “It doesn’t work, in my opinion, because if you say that you’re going to end up in a world where everyone’s agent is attacking everyone’s with no clear kind of responsibility.”

He declined to comment on some specific legislation, including an AI liability proposal in California but said the government has a role to play in mandating disclosures of cyber incidents.

“I think there’s a lot to do around how to create better disclosures,” including what information needs to be disclosed and when it should be disclosed, he said.

creator: Owen Dahlkamp

title: Anthropic policy chief says winning AI race key for safety
content:
Anthropic’s policy chief Sarah Heck said Wednesday that the U.S. can’t make artificial intelligence safer if it falls behind China in the global tech race.

“The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI, and you can’t do safety from second place,” the head of public policy said at POLITICO’s Decoded summit in Washington, echoing an argument often made by President Donald Trump and his advisers.

Heck’s comments made the case for export controls on the sale of AI chips to China. She repeatedly defended Anthropic as having a long history of being motivated by safety concerns and said it’s focused on working with lawmakers to pass new regulations for the technology.

“We do think it’s existential to do this. We do think we have to balance the risk now,” Heck said. “The capabilities are only increasing and increasing at a pace that is accelerating.”
snippet: Anthropic’s policy chief Sarah Heck said Wednesday that the U.S. can’t make artificial intelligence safer if it falls behind China in the global tech race.
creator: Gabby Miller, Christine Mui

title: Von der Leyen’s call for talks on pausing AI can’t quell extinction risk fears
content:
STRASBOURG — Ursula von der Leyen has declared herself an AI “optimist.” Yet in the face of rising warnings of the technology’s threats to humanity, the European Commission president on Wednesday sounded far more like a realist — and one with limited room for maneuver.

Von der Leyen didn’t shy away from the topic in her State of the European Union address, calling AI one of the “two tipping points of our time” and acknowledging the dangers it poses.

“The warnings about the future of AI should make us more serious about safety,” said key European Parliament AI lawmaker Axel Voss after the speech, touting von der Leyen’s focus on “Europe’s human-centered approach to AI.”

Still, the Commission president’s most concrete response to recent calls by top Silicon Valley bosses to pause AI development was a cordial invitation to join her in a “discussion” on the matter.

And while citing the EU’s standing AI rules as a possible building block for global regulations, von der Leyen didn’t use her much-anticipated speech to call on fellow world leaders — particularly U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping — to come together to act.

title: Nvidia boss on AI safety: ‘We don’t need any new laws’
content:
SAN FRANCISCO — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the AI industry doesn’t need any new laws Tuesday during San Francisco’s annual Dreamforce megaconference hosted by Salesforce billionaire Marc Benioff, doubling down on arguments that have also been voiced by President Donald Trump.

“We don’t need any new laws. We don’t need new regulations,” Huang, one of the leading luminaries of the AI industry as head of one of the most profitable companies, said during an interview with the Salesforce CEO.

His comments at one of San Francisco’s biggest tech conferences highlighted the divide among industry leaders over AI safety, after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off a political firestorm over the weekend with his calls to slow the pace of AI development. Huang spoke just minutes after Amodei also did with Benioff, who congratulated him on his company’s development of AI technology being increasingly plugged into Salesforce.

title: OpenAI backs bipartisan push to address AI biothreats
content:
OpenAI is supporting a slate of bills that the company says will help prevent artificial intelligence models from supercharging the threat of biological weapons and synthetic viruses.

The bills aim to improve access to data needed to build AI defenses against synthetic and naturally occurring biothreats, and establish standards for the safe development of those tools.

The company exclusively told POLITICO that it is issuing new endorsements for three bipartisan bills surrounding the issue: the Web of Biological Data Act, and the AI-Ready Bio-Data Standards Act and the SCALE Biology Act. The first two proposals were previously introduced in both the House and Senate, the latter in the House.

OpenAI’s endorsement marks an expansion of the company’s push for legislation addressing both the risks AI could pose to biological security and the defensive technology it could help create, as public concern about the destructive potential of advanced AI models rises. Earlier Tuesday, the company said it would back a bipartisan House proposal requiring top AI companies to embed outside evaluators to ensure their models are safe.
snippet: OpenAI is supporting a slate of bills that the company says will help prevent artificial intelligence models from supercharging the threat of biological weapons and synthetic viruses.
creator: Aaron Mak

title: OpenAI: AI capabilities are in a ‘different place’ and require urgency
content:
President Donald Trump called AI concerns a “hoax.” One of the country’s leading AI companies said Tuesday it’s hoping Washington will still act.

OpenAI, which this weekend called for federal safety measures alongside its rival Anthropic, said it spent the beginning of the week meeting with members of both parties to discuss legislation that would rein in AI developers as warnings of impending doom, job loss and massive cyberattacks become increasingly prevalent.

Models are developing at breakneck speed and agents are acting in ways that engineers are struggling to predict or control. Even as there have long been calls for regulation, recent hacks of companies such as Hugging Face have engendered fresh waves of concern that the technology is reaching a point in which it is capable of causing serious harm.

“We have certainly conveyed that really over the last month that capabilities are in a different place, and as a result of those capabilities being in a different place, we do feel like there needs to be an urgency to this,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, said the company told the White House.
snippet: President Donald Trump called AI concerns a “hoax.” One of the country’s leading AI companies said Tuesday it’s hoping Washington will still act.
creator: Cheyenne Haslett

title: EU countries to discuss AI rules as Trump calls safety warnings a ‘hoax’
content:
Government officials from across the European Union will gather in Brussels on Thursday to discuss how to set global rules to counter the threat from new AI models, according to two EU diplomats and a draft agenda seen by POLITICO.

The European Commission will give “updates on EU and international AI policy” and give a “technical briefing on recent AI incidents” during a gathering of the Artificial Intelligence Board, which comprises of representatives from every EU member country and regularly convenes to monitor progress on the bloc’s Artificial Intelligence Act.

This week’s gathering follows a series of calls to slow down AI development by top company leaders such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman. U.S. President Donald Trump immediately rebuffed the calls, calling the AI safety warnings a “hoax” and arguing that slowing down would give China the momentum in AI.

The European discussions on global cooperation will focus on work done at the G7, the G20 and the United Nations, one of the diplomats said.

Last Friday, the European Commission’s top tech official, Executive Vice President for Tech Sovereignty Henna Virkkunen, called for global AI rules and cooperation.

title: Carney puts exclamation point on Europe courtship with French archipelago visit
content:
PARIS — Mark Carney will wrap up a week spent shifting his country’s foreign policy toward Europe on Sunday with the first-ever visit by a Canadian prime minister to the obscure French territory of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, where he’ll meet President Emmanuel Macron.

The trip to the picturesque archipelago — a few kilometers off the south coast of the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador and home to fewer than 6,000 people — comes after Carney travels to Strasbourg for Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union speech on Wednesday. The Canadian leader then journeys on to Liverpool to meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Carney and Macron will discuss cooperation on AI, energy, defense and critical minerals, according to a statement from the Canadian prime minister’s office. It is also Macron’s first trip there since taking office in 2017.

While Carney has for months sought to move Ottawa closer to Brussels and Paris as part of his middle powers alliance against the U.S. under President Donald Trump, the pivot has taken on renewed urgency amid the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen each side slap reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars worth of goods.

title: Von der Leyen’s warring EU Parliament allies want her to pick a side. Can she appease them?
content:
STRASBOURG — The two biggest factions in the European Parliament want completely different things from Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech on Wednesday. If she can’t keep them both happy, the rift between these traditional centrist allies risks becoming a chasm as the far-right makes gains across the continent.

The center-right wants von der Leyen to double down on the simplification drive of the past two years while further toughening the bloc’s stance on migration in the wake of the Ceuta crisis. The center-left, meanwhile, wants a halt to what it calls the deregulation of EU green policies, and for von der Leyen to steer the center-right away from passing measures in the Parliament with far-right votes.

“We expect your address to send a clear political commitment that there will be no backtracking on the European Green Deal,” Iratxe García Pérez, president of the S&D group in the European Parliament, told von der Leyen in a letter, calling for “a change of focus away from deregulation.”

title: ‘SICK conspiracy going on against AI’: Trump bids to shut down regulation push
content:
President Donald Trump tried to shut down a burgeoning push for the United States to further regulate artificial intelligence on Monday morning, saying the U.S. has already done enough to prevent AI from catastrophic risks.

The post comes as technology leaders called for the industry to slow down the production of artificial intelligence over the weekend, sending tech stocks tumbling on Monday.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

He added, “there is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”
snippet: President Donald Trump tried to shut down a burgeoning push for the United States to further regulate artificial intelligence on Monday morning, saying the U.S. has already done enough to prevent AI

title: ‘Horror in the sky’: Ukraine races for a solution to Russian jet-powered drones
content:
KYIV — Russia is upgrading its attack drones by powering them with fast turbojet engines, making them much more difficult to intercept and forcing Ukraine to develop technology to knock them down.

The shift is adding to the strain on a country already accustomed to nights spent under air-raid alerts: faster drones give air-defense crews less time to respond, can outpace the defenses that helped counter earlier Shaheds and threaten homes, transport and critical infrastructure across Ukraine.

“Together with dozens of Ukrainian companies, we are already looking for cheap and mass-produced solutions, in particular for intercepting jet-powered drones. Some interceptors are already undergoing combat testing,” Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara said last week at a meeting of Ukraine’s allies.

“We cannot simply wait while Russia refines its repertoire of killings. Right now, we need to focus as much attention as possible on securing the skies, finding ways to protect people, and scaling up our response to Russian drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last Friday.
snippet: KYIV — Russia is upgrading its attack drones by powering them with fast turbojet engines, making them much more difficult to intercept and forcing Ukraine to develop technology to knock them down.
creator: Veronika Melkozerova

title: Von der Leyen to skip Carney speech in EU Parliament
content:
STRASBOURG — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will not attend Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s address to the European Parliament on Thursday. 

Carney will speak to lawmakers on Thursday at 11.30 a.m. as he seeks closer ties with the EU amid deteriorating relations with Washington. He is expected to set out his wishlist for Brussels ahead of a Canada-EU summit in October. The address comes a day after he will attend von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union speech.

During Carney’s speech, the Commission will instead be represented by Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič — one of von der Leyen’s most trusted lieutenants — the executive’s chief spokesperson Paula Pinho confirmed.

The Commission president won’t be in Strasbourg on Thursday as she has to return to Brussels due to “prior commitments,” Pinho said. One of those prior commitments is a press conference on the child online safety initiative.
snippet: STRASBOURG — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will not attend Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s address to the European Parliament on Thursday.
creator: Max Griera

title: EU to limit access to social media before age of 15
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission will propose new rules to restrict minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms before the age of 15, according to preparatory documents seen by POLITICO and a person familiar with the matter.

The EU executive on Thursday will unveil a new EU KIDS Act setting out age restrictions, along with new rules requiring covered products, such as social media and AI companions, to be safe by design. The proposal aims to create a tiered system for accessing social media under parental supervision before age 15, the documents said.

The age restrictions are a major step by the European Commission and its President Ursula von der Leyen to better safeguard minors’ on social media platforms, amid a fierce backlash from health experts, politicians and parents against the effects of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and others on the mental health of minors.

It comes after months of intense pressure from government leaders, including France’s Emmanuel Macron, to put the issue at the top of the political agenda. Austria, Denmark, France, Greece and Spain are all pushing ahead with national laws to restrict kids’ access to social media.

title: The ideas shaping von der Leyen’s pitch to Carney
content:
From defense to critical raw materials, a new wave of EU-Canada agreements is on the horizon.

By MAX GRIERA, CAMILLE GIJS, GABRIEL GAVIN and
GERARDO FORTUNA in Brussels

Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

The EU is looking to pull Canada closer into its economic and security orbit as Donald Trump’s trade war forces Ottawa to seek allies beyond the U.S.

The offer under discussion spans critical minerals, digital trade, education, skilled workers and Arctic security. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney due to address the European Parliament this week and an EU-Canada summit set for October in Montreal, EU officials are weighing what Ursula von der Leyen can concretely offer in her State of the Union speech on Wednesday.

The aim is to deepen cooperation wherever it benefits both sides — and give Carney a way to show Canadians that Ottawa has powerful friends beyond Washington, 15 officials, politicians and diplomats told POLITICO.

The most ambitious proposals would bring Canada closer to the EU’s single market, expanding its existing trade ties with the bloc and moving it toward the level of integration enjoyed by nations such as Switzerland and Norway.
snippet:
From defense to critical raw materials, a new wave of EU-Canada agreements is on the horizon.

By MAX GRIERA, CAMILLE GIJS, GABRIEL GAVIN and GERARDO FORTUNA in Brussels
creator: Max Griera, Camille Gijs, Gabriel Gavin, Gerardo Fortuna

title: How to write a State of the Union speech
content:
Big promises, special guests and social media influencers have become a routine part of the EU’s most high-profile address.

By GABRIEL GAVIN
in Brussels

Illustration by Arnau Busquets Guàrdia/POLITICO

For the past six months, officials across Brussels have been feeding ideas, demands and policy pledges into Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech. Its contents, however, will remain a closely guarded secret until the European Commission president takes the podium on Wednesday.

The speech is the product of a sprawling process involving Commission departments, national officials, experts, lobbyists and interest groups. Yet the final decisions — what makes the cut, what is discarded and what becomes the central message — are made by a tiny circle around the president.

“There was a process where everybody would ask for something,” said Margaritis Schinas, a former Commission vice-president who helped prepare previous addresses. “But there was also a process where the president and the cabinet and ourselves were very clear on the few things to harvest that would make an impact.”

title: How did von der Leyen’s ‘independence moment’ hold up over 12 months?
content:
Ursula von der Leyen used her set piece speech last year to declare Europe’s “independence moment.” Twelve months later, the European Commission president’s record shows the EU’s independence still very much depends on its national capitals.

One year after her last State of the Union address, von der Leyen has delivered most clearly where the Commission could act largely on its own: writing laws and funding initiatives on core topics like tech, trade and social policy.

She struggled most where success required member countries to agree, surrender more control to Brussels or build genuinely new European capabilities — particularly on defense.

“The issue of defense plays a completely different role in Europe than it did just two years ago,” said Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, the liberal chair of the European Parliament’s security and defense committee, pointing to a series of “very valuable programs” launched over the past year.

But, she added, “all efforts are reaching their limits, because national self-interest continues to play a major role.”

That tension runs through POLITICO’s assessment of the promises in von der Leyen’s last State of the Union address.

title: ‘I don’t have any’: Trump brushes aside concerns over AI’s existential risks
content:
President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about the catastrophic risks of artificial intelligence raised this week by some AI researchers, saying late Thursday he was focused instead on the U.S. losing its edge in the tech arms race.

Asked whether he has concerns about existential risks posed by AI, the president said, “No, I don’t have any.

“I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position,” Trump told reporters late Thursday as he left Dallas. “We are leading China right now by a pretty good period.”

Trump was wading into a debate over AI’s catastrophic risks ignited by a viral social media post from a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher. The post cautioned that the leading AI companies have been “gambling with our lives” and that some researchers working on the technology “believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

The post and the discourse it stirred up — along with recent alarming incidents where AI agents have gone rogue to launch hacking attacks — have prompted fresh calls from bipartisan lawmakers to rein in the fast-evolving technology.

title: Jensen Huang: Don’t regulate AI like social media
content:
AYRSHIRE, SCOTLAND — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI should not be regulated like social media because AI is a “technology” rather than a “product.”

Speaking at an AI event convened by King Charles III at Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland, Huang told journalists that AI is “very different than social media” and that at present the security issues involving AI are “related to products not ready to be released.”

His remarks come as governments around the world are grappling with whether to place regulatory constraints on AI, and after AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have called for a slowing of AI development.

“Unlike social media, which is a product, AI is a technology that’s behind all of these other tech, all of these products — and so, regulate the products,” Huang said.

He said authorities should monitor for when an AI deployment “goes wrong” and “whenever new laws are necessary, add to the existing laws,” but pointed out that there are existing regulations in sectors where AI is deployed such healthcare, transportation, and entertainment.
snippet: AYRSHIRE, SCOTLAND — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI should not be regulated like social media because AI is a “technology” rather than a “product.”
creator: Frank Hersey, Joseph Bambridge

title: Canada’s Carney stops short of endorsing von der Leyen’s associate member plan
content:
STRASBOURG — Mark Carney used an address to the European Parliament to sketch out what Ottawa would want from closer ties with the EU but declined to give full-throated approval of Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise “associate member” plan.

Speaking a day after the Commission president floated the unique relationship status, the Canadian prime minister acknowledged the offer and instead of accepting it outright, listed potential individual areas of cooperation, including critical minerals, defense, AI, energy security, and space.

He also called for more seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and services, as well as Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program.

“We welcome this ambition,” he said, after name-checking the idea of von der Leyen, who was sitting in the audience. “Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties.”

Carney’s list of potential tie-ups was an early attempt to put substance behind what, for now, remains a largely undefined political proposition.

title: OpenAI finds 6 new cases of ‘concerning’ AI behavior
content:
Artificial intelligence frontrunner OpenAI on Thursday announced it found evidence that its agents behaved at odds with human goals and values, adding to concerns over the safety of cutting-edge AI systems.

In six separate incidents, OpenAI agents either concealed information from human engineers or instructed themselves not to act as someone’s assistant while trained or tested, the company said.

OpenAI also rolled out a new framework to track, investigate and disclose any “unexpected or concerning model behavior,” known as “misalignment” failures. The tech firm now has a clear disclosure procedure, wherein any employee can flag model misalignment, after which it can be considered for public disclosure.

AI models going rogue have sparked global backlash after researchers from inside leading AI firms warned that the technology could make humanity go extinct. AI bosses like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have called on industry and governments to slow down AI development.
snippet: Artificial intelligence frontrunner OpenAI on Thursday announced it found evidence that its agents behaved at odds with human goals and values, adding to concerns over the safety of cutting-edge AI

title: ‘AI has been marketed horribly,’ LinkedIn co-founder says
content:
LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman admitted on Wednesday that artificial intelligence has been mismarketed to Americans, even as he sees a narrow lane for a tech optimist to win them back in 2028.

“AI has been marketed horribly to the American people,” Hoffman said during POLITICO’s Decoded Summit in Washington.

Hoffman said that if a candidate helps Americans understand how AI could economically benefit them amid rising gas and food prices, then “there’s a lane for presidential candidates to be more AI positive.” He added that a different approach is needed from the current messaging he sees around data centers.

But Hoffman also said that AI and tech optimism are not necessary to earn his personal support in 2028.

“How I operate politically is I don’t actually in fact say ‘Oh, I’m only supporting you if you support my pet cause,’” he said. He added: “Let’s support rule of law. Let’s not have blatant lies around election denialism.”

title: ‘We absolutely can’t surrender,’ top Republican says of AI race with China
content:
House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie said Wednesday that he agrees serious concerns exist about the growing power of artificial intelligence — but warned against adopting the kinds of strict regulations that he argues have depressed tech advances in Europe.

“If you want to say, ‘We’re just gonna turn this over to a handful of elite educated people in a room … well, that’s how Europe’s run,” the Kentucky Republican said during the POLITICO Decoded Summit in Washington. He added that such a system would give just a few leading AI developers disproportionate regulatory power and limit other companies’ ability to compete, “and I don’t think that’s a good path to have.”

He added that whatever guardrails Washington adopts must not limit the industry in a manner that could hinder the United States’ standing in the global AI race with China.

“We absolutely can’t surrender,” Guthrie said. “And I think that’s what it would be if we stopped AI development.”

title: EU antitrust chief would consider request from AI firms to coordinate on safety
content:
STRASBOURG — EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said Wednesday she would consider giving artificial intelligence companies more room to coordinate on safety without falling foul of antitrust law. 

Yet so far, she said, none of them has asked.

“We have not got a formal request, at least for the time being,” Ribera told reporters. “But I think that this is an interesting question and we will have to dive into this proposal if it comes.”

EU rules already allow rivals to work together in some cases where there is a public interest, she said, as long as the conditions are spelled out and regulators are told.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei put the question on the table last Saturday, arguing that the leading labs should settle on common safety standards and “limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

To do that lawfully, he wrote, the U.S. government would have to “issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations.” 

Within hours OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had all independently backed him.

The debate over AI safety standards has also made it to Strasbourg.
snippet: STRASBOURG — EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said Wednesday she would consider giving artificial intelligence companies more room to coordinate on safety without falling foul of antitrust law.
creator: Gerardo Fortuna, Jacob Parry

title: 12 takeaways from von der Leyen’s State of the Union
content:
Ursula von der Leyen used her State of the Union speech to unveil a raft of proposals aimed at making Europe better prepared for a world of threats — from sweltering summers to hybrid warfare, migrant crises and social media.

What the Commission president chose to talk about in Strasbourg — and, just as importantly, what she left unsaid — will help define the rest of her term and the political legacy she leaves behind.

Here are the 12 biggest takeaways.

The biggest surprise came when von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member.”

Speaking directly to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was sitting in the Parliament hemicycle, von der Leyen proposed an ambitious, far-reaching new alliance spanning tech, defense, energy, critical minerals, AI, the Arctic and more.

In a message that could have been addressed directly to U.S. President Donald Trump, von der Leyen said: “This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

title: Poll: Americans say there’s a serious risk of AI destroying humanity
content:
A majority of Americans think artificial intelligence could someday destroy humanity.

The stunning new finding from The POLITICO Poll underscores the depth of people’s anxieties about the rapidly developing technology — and how quickly public sentiment around AI has hardened. Just a few months ago, AI was a nebulous concept for many Americans. Now, lawmakers in both parties are racing to understand how to control its growth.

Overall, about two out of three Americans say there is at least a “moderate” risk that advanced AI could destroy humanity, with majorities across parties, genders and age groups holding that view. Americans who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 are somewhat more likely to see such a risk (70%) than those who voted for President Donald Trump (60%).

Those fears have burst into public view in recent days after the leaders of the nation’s top AI labs — Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — called with Elon Musk for slowing the pace of advanced AI development. The rare show of agreement from some of the industry’s fiercest competitors pushed long-simmering warnings about the technology’s dangers into the center of public debate.
snippet: A majority of Americans think artificial intelligence could someday destroy humanity.
creator: Erin Doherty

title: EU capitals caught off guard as von der Leyen announces ‘associate membership’ for Canada
content:
BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s announcement that the EU will explore “associate membership” for Canada came as a surprise to member countries — and left governments concerned about the potential trade-offs.

During her annual State of the Union speech in Strasbourg, von der Leyen floated the upgrading of relations with Ottawa to meet the need to “urgently reimagine our partnerships” and “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies.”

Canada, which is locked in an escalating trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, will begin “opening the door” to become “the first associate member of the EU.”

But the message wrong-footed national capitals, which were never asked to sign off on the idea before the speech, said three diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. Granting membership to the EU is a responsibility of the European Council, and no model for associate membership exists.

title: Von der Leyen tries to stem tide on global threats ― from Trump to AI and climate
content:
STRASBOURG ― Ursula von der Leyen used her State of the Union speech Wednesday to rally against a world that’s making Europe less powerful and poorer, and to which artificial intelligence and climate change present existential risks.

In a longer and more passionate speech than the EU has been used to, the European Commission president made the case for “independence” ― economically, militarily and technologically.

“Europe has chosen to forge its own path,” she said, in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, alongside special guest Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who shares many of the same perspectives for his country. This was a “complex age of great possibilities and great perils,” she said.

While in previous years, the Commission president’s annual address has been about a list of ideas and policies the EU should implement, this time a combination of more fragile national governments and the myriad challenges facing the world meant von der Leyen sounded more like she was delivering a direct appeal to Europeans about what kind of place they want to live in.

title: EU wants Canada to become ‘associate member,’ von der Leyen says
content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wants Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union, she said in her annual State of the Union address on Wednesday.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen said her speech to European lawmakers, which was attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Von der Leyen also announced a comprehensive new “Alliance for the Future,” built on the existing EU-Canada trade deal that would “create a common prosperity and economic security space.”

The nine-year-old CETA accord has, however, yet to be ratified by national and regional parliaments in 10 EU member states.

Von der Leyen’s initiative comes as Brussels and Ottawa seek to forge closer ties while both grapple with a costly trade war with the United States. Von der Leyen nonetheless insisted that the new partnership is “not against anyone else.”
snippet: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wants Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union, she said in her annual State of the Union address on Wednesday.
creator: Camille Gijs, Gabriel Gavin

title: Von der Leyen will invite AI leaders to discuss how to ‘pace the frontier’
content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen plans to invite the main artificial intelligence companies to discuss industry efforts to impose a slowdown of AI development, she said in her State of the European Union speech on Wednesday.

“I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier,” she said.

Von der Leyen acknowledged the safety warnings by several top tech bosses in the past week, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call for a slowdown that quickly got the backing of the CEO of xAI Elon Musk and OpenAI chief Sam Altman.

Von der Leyen did not offer an explicit assessment on those calls, but said Europe was ready to “support ongoing industry efforts” on it.

The Commission president also called for international collaboration on the testing and evaluating of frontier AI models. She is expected to extend that invitation to the U.K. and Canada, but refrained from mentioning the U.S. and China, the clear frontrunners in the AI race.

title: EU-China trade deficit has hit ‘tipping point,’ warns von der Leyen
content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will use her State of the Union speech on Wednesday to reiterate her warning over the EU’s ballooning trade deficit with China, as Brussels steps up negotiations with Beijing ahead of a key October deadline.

“Our trade deficit with China is now €1 billion euro — a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she was due to tell lawmakers in Strasbourg, according to her prepared remarks obtained in advance by POLITICO.

“Some say the second China shock is looming. But it’s already here. It shows in our communities and factories across our Union. It leads to de-industrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable,” she said.

“This is why we are engaged in a dialogue with China to rebalance our trade,” von der Leyen added. “But this dialogue must now lead to results. China’s weaker domestic demand means it also needs our European market. So, it is in both our interests to work together to find solutions.”

The Commission president’s speech gave no detail, however, on the actual steps Brussels was prepared to take to protect European industry from what it sees as unfair competition.

title: Why the EU and Canada are betting on an AI ‘middle powers’ play
content:
BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed a new “tech alliance” between the EU and Canada in her State of the Union. During his own speech Thursday to the European Parliament, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared that the two sides should “join forces” on AI safety and pooling compute power.

Yet even before the public displays of connection in Strasbourg, there’s already plenty bringing Canada and Europe together on the AI front. Both lag behind the U.S. and China in AI development and compute power, and thus lack the political clout to set the direction and pace of global regulation. Together, however, Brussels and Ottawa could maybe — just maybe — compete for leadership in the development and policing of this emerging and powerful technology.

It is Carney’s “middle powers” pitch in action.

title: 7 things Ursula von der Leyen will say in her State of the Union speech
content:
Here’s what the European Commission president will announce in her biggest address of the year.

By SEBASTIAN STARCEVIC
in Brussels

Photo-Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO

Ursula von der Leyen has pegged her political legacy to making Europe more independent in a dangerous world. On Wednesday, the European Commission president will have to explain how that’s going — and what’s next.

As the EU deals with wars, wildfires and Donald Trump, von der Leyen will use her sixth State of the Union speech to lay out her agenda: climate-proofing Europe; catching up with China and the U.S. on artificial intelligence; turbocharging the bloc’s defense industry; and reforming its migration rules.

The speech will be revised and rewritten right up to the point she delivers it. But based on conversations with more than a dozen European officials, granted anonymity to discuss the president’s priorities and talking points, here’s what POLITICO’s newsroom has heard she will say.
